newsitem.title: CHINA: China jobless seen rising to 5.9 mln at year-end.
newsitem.headline: China jobless seen rising to 5.9 mln at year-end.

text.p: The number of official urban jobless in China is expected to rise to 5.9 million by the end of this year, compared with 5.3 million at the end of March, the China Daily said on Tuesday.

The Ministry of Labour has issued a directive ordering provincial departments to create new jobs to try to accommodate at least half of those without work, the newspaper quoted Minister Li Boyong as saying.
In the next few years, the number of people looking for jobs in China will increase sharply, Li said.

In urban areas alone, work needs to be found for 13.7 million people while there are jobs for only 7.8 million, Li said. Unemployment was therefore expected to hit 5.9 million by the end of this year.

The official number of China's urban jobless reached 5.3 million at the end of March, or about 3.0 percent. That figure consists only of urban workers without jobs and who have asked the government to help them find work.

If the 7.5 million employees of state enterprises that have stopped or cut production were included, the actual urban unemployment rate would be about 4.5 percent, officials of the State Statistical Bureau have said.
China has about 15 million surplus workers, who do not officially count as unemployed.
Officials have said that at least 54 million public employees -- or 36 percent of the entire state payroll -- are actually considered surplus labour.
Urban unemployment could soar as high as 15-20 million by the end of the century as China battles to revive struggling state enterprises, many of them burdened with an inflated workforce.
Labour Minister Li warned that unemployment would rise because the government has expanded to 111 from 58 the number of pilot cities experimenting with bankruptcy to revive debt-laden state firms.
China's leaders have for years postponed introducing tough reforms to revive state firms because of deep-seated fears that a rising number of jobless could spark social unrest.
A major official newspaper called on Monday for an easing of China's tight monetary policy, saying Beijing needed to boost investment and create jobs for millions of unemployed workers.

"The focus of our macroeconomic policy should change direction from economic stability to economic development," the official Economic Daily said in a rare departure from the official party line that the tight squeeze is essential.
China tightened credit and curbed investment in 1993 to rein in galloping inflation, slowing down rapid economic growth for the sake of economic stability.
Chinese authorities would need to find jobs for 160-180 million workers between 1996 and 2000, the newspaper said.
"There is a danger that the situation would unceasingly worsen," the newspaper said, adding that a planned unemployment relief fund was not the solution to the problem.
